marrow__BIOCHEM_CH26_Q001.takeaway: mRNA carries protein-coding information from DNA to the ribosome, where its codons specify the amino-acid sequence.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH26_Q001.displayText:
mRNA carries protein-coding information from DNA to the ribosome, where its codons specify the amino-acid sequence.

mRNA is a protein-coding RNA.
The mRNA convey genetic information from DNA to the ribosome, where they specify the amino
acid sequence of the protein products of gene expression.
emphasis: mRNA carries protein-coding information from DNA to the ribosome, where its codons specify the amino-acid sequence

rationales.b: tRNA is an adaptor that delivers amino acids and reads codons; its RNA sequence does not encode the protein product.
rationales.c: rRNA forms the structural and catalytic core of ribosomes but is not translated into protein.
rationales.d: snRNA participates in pre-mRNA splicing, not direct protein coding.

sourceNotes: Source question/key: ED8 Biochemistry p. 404; explanation p. 410.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH26_Q002.takeaway: miRNA regulates gene expression by binding target mRNAs; mRNA, rRNA and tRNA act directly in translation.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH26_Q002.displayText:
miRNA regulates gene expression by binding target mRNAs; mRNA, rRNA and tRNA act directly in translation.

miRNA is not directly involved in protein synthesis. miRNA participates in the modulation of
gene expression by altering mRNA function.
The mRNAs, rRNAs, and tRNAs are directly involved in protein synthesis. Other RNAs participate
in either mRNA splicing (snRNAs) or modulation of gene expression by altering mRNA function
(mi/siRNAs) and/or expression (IncRNAs).
emphasis: miRNA regulates gene expression by binding target mRNAs; mRNA, rRNA and tRNA act directly in translation

rationales.a: mRNA supplies the codon sequence read by ribosomes during protein synthesis.
rationales.b: rRNA forms the ribosome's structural and catalytic framework needed for peptide synthesis.
rationales.c: tRNA carries amino acids to the ribosome and pairs its anticodon with mRNA codons.

sourceNotes: Source question/key: ED8 Biochemistry p. 404; explanation p. 411.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH26_Q004.takeaway: DNA-dependent RNA polymerase reads a DNA template and polymerizes complementary ribonucleotides to make RNA.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH26_Q004.displayText:
DNA-dependent RNA polymerase reads a DNA template and polymerizes complementary ribonucleotides to make RNA.

DNA-dependent RNA polymerase is the enzyme responsible for the polymerization of
ribonucleotides into a sequence complementary to the template strand of the gene.
The enzyme attaches at a specific site, the promoter, on the template strand. This is followed by
the initiation of RNA synthesis at the starting point, and the process continues until a termination
sequence is reached.
emphasis: DNA-dependent RNA polymerase reads a DNA template and polymerizes complementary ribonucleotides to make RNA

rationales.a: RNA-dependent RNA polymerase copies RNA from an RNA template, as in some viruses, not a gene's DNA template.
rationales.b: DNA-dependent RNA convertase is not the standard enzyme name for transcription.
rationales.c: RNA-dependent replicase uses an RNA template to replicate RNA rather than transcribing a DNA gene.

sourceNotes: Source question/key: ED8 Biochemistry p. 404,405; explanation p. 411.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH26_Q005.takeaway: Topoisomerases relieve torsional strain and supercoils that arise as RNA polymerase opens and traverses DNA.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH26_Q005.displayText:
Topoisomerases relieve torsional strain and supercoils that arise as RNA polymerase opens and traverses DNA.

Topoisomerase prevents the formation of superhelical tensions in the DNA during transcription.
During transcription, supercoils form when the DNA is unwound and can add stress to the
molecule. Topoisomerase activity enables RNA elongation to proceed further without being
stopped. This action of topoisomerase also takes place during DNA replication.
emphasis: Topoisomerases relieve torsional strain and supercoils that arise as RNA polymerase opens and traverses DNA

rationales.b: RNA polymerase synthesizes RNA but does not remove the superhelical stress created by transcription.
rationales.c: Pyrophosphatases hydrolyze pyrophosphate and do not relax DNA supercoils.
rationales.d: DNA strand separation is performed by helicase in replication; topoisomerases relieve torsional stress during transcription.

sourceNotes: Source question/key: ED8 Biochemistry p. 405; explanation p. 411,412.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH26_Q006.takeaway: RNA polymerase II makes pre-mRNA and many snRNAs/miRNAs; RNA polymerase I transcribes the major rRNAs.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH26_Q006.displayText:
RNA polymerase II makes pre-mRNA and many snRNAs/miRNAs; RNA polymerase I transcribes the major rRNAs.

Synthesis of rRNA is not a function of RNA polymerase II. This is done by RNA polymerase I
emphasis: RNA polymerase II makes pre-mRNA and many snRNAs/miRNAs; RNA polymerase I transcribes the major rRNAs

rationales.a: RNA polymerase II synthesizes protein-coding pre-mRNA in eukaryotes.
rationales.c: Many microRNAs are transcribed by RNA polymerase II from longer precursors.
rationales.d: Several small nuclear RNAs are transcribed by RNA polymerase II; the listed rRNA synthesis is the exception.

sourceNotes: Source question/key: ED8 Biochemistry p. 405; explanation p. 412.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH26_Q007.takeaway: Bacterial sigma factor recognizes promoter sequences and positions core RNA polymerase for transcription initiation.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH26_Q007.displayText:
Bacterial sigma factor recognizes promoter sequences and positions core RNA polymerase for transcription initiation.

The o subunit (sigma factor) enables RNA polymerase to recognize promoter regions on the DNA
and thus helps to position it correctly on the template DNA. & ’
ae n%
emphasis: Bacterial sigma factor recognizes promoter sequences and positions core RNA polymerase for transcription initiation

rationales.a: The core RNA polymerase catalyzes phosphodiester-bond formation; sigma mainly provides promoter recognition.
rationales.c: Sigma factor facilitates initiation and often dissociates after promoter escape; it is not the termination factor.
rationales.d: RNA polymerase and associated factors open promoter DNA; sigma's key role is promoter targeting, not acting as helicase.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH26_Q009.takeaway: RNA polymerase II is coupled to pre-mRNA processing and termination factors; its CTD helps coordinate transcript termination and polyadenylation.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH26_Q009.displayText:
RNA polymerase II is coupled to pre-mRNA processing and termination factors; its CTD helps coordinate transcript termination and polyadenylation.

RNA polymerase gives signals for the termination of RNA transcription. Proteins catalyzing RNA processing, termination, and polyadenylation appear to load onto RNA polymerase II soon after initiation.
Termination of transcription can be:
• ρ dependent: When the termination signals are met, ρ factor binds to RNA. ρ factor has ATP-dependent helicase activity. It detaches the RNA from the DNA.
• ρ independent: In the 3′ end of RNA, there is a series of U. RNA detaches from DNA due to weaker A=U at the end.
emphasis: RNA polymerase II is coupled to pre-mRNA processing and termination factors; its CTD helps coordinate transcript termination and polyadenylation

rationales.a: RNA polymerase I transcribes the large rRNA precursor; the question's processing/termination association is with Pol II.
rationales.c: RNA polymerase III transcribes tRNAs and 5S rRNA; Pol II CTD recruits the mRNA processing machinery described.
rationales.d: Topoisomerase manages DNA topology, not transcription termination signaling.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH26_Q010.takeaway: The coding (non-template) DNA strand matches the RNA sequence except that DNA has T where RNA has U: 5′-TAAGGC-3′.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH26_Q010.displayText:
The coding (non-template) DNA strand matches the RNA sequence except that DNA has T where RNA has U: 5′-TAAGGC-3′.

The non-template strand or coding strand in the DNA will have the same sequence of the RNA
that is produced, except that the non-template or coding strand has T is in place of U.
As all sequences are written in the 5’ to 3’ direction, unless otherwise specified, an RNA sequence
of UAAGGC would correspond to a DNA sequence, on the non-template strand, of TAAGGC. Both
the non-template strand and RNA produced will be a complementary sequence to the template
strand. Therefore, the template strand would be ATTCCG (written 5’ to 3’).

rationales.b: RNA uses U; the DNA coding strand must use T at that position.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH26_Q012.takeaway: The 5′ 7-methylguanosine cap promotes RNA processing and translation initiation and protects mRNA from 5′ exonucleases.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH26_Q012.displayText:
The 5′ 7-methylguanosine cap promotes RNA processing and translation initiation and protects mRNA from 5′ exonucleases.

7-methyl-guanosine triphosphate capping of primary transcript is necessary for:
* Processing of the primary transcript to mRNA
¢ Translation of the mRNA
+ Protection of the mRNA against nucleolytic attack by 5’-exonucleases
emphasis: The 5′ 7-methylguanosine cap promotes RNA processing and translation initiation and protects mRNA from 5′ exonucleases

rationales.a: The cap helps pre-mRNA processing and export, but its functions extend beyond maturation alone.
rationales.b: The cap is recognized by translation initiation machinery and supports ribosome recruitment.
rationales.c: The cap protects the 5′ end against exonucleolytic degradation; it also has processing and translation functions.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH26_Q016.takeaway: Self-splicing introns catalyze their own removal through RNA folding and transesterification without a spliceosome protein catalyst.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH26_Q016.displayText:
Self-splicing introns catalyze their own removal through RNA folding and transesterification without a spliceosome protein catalyst.

Self-splicing introns do not require a spliceosome or any other proteins for the splicing reaction.
Self-splicing introns fold into complex loops and undergo transesterification reactions, thus
undergoing self splicing.
Other options:
Option A: Split genes have the advantage that they allow alternative splicing so that a single gene
can code for variant forms of the same protein.
Option C: B-thalassemia results from the faulty splicing of the B-globin transcript. However, the
spliceosome is normal and the reason for the fault is a mutation in the B-globin gene itself.
Option D: Splicing occurs in the nucleus and mature transcripts are then transported into the
cytosol for translation (protein synthesis) to occur.

rationales.c: β-thalassemia can result from mutations that alter splice sites, but that is not evidence of a universal spliceosome defect.
rationales.d: Most nuclear pre-mRNA splicing occurs in the nucleus, not the cytosol.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH26_Q019.takeaway: eEF-2 uses GTP to translocate peptidyl-tRNA and the ribosome along mRNA during elongation.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH26_Q019.displayText:
eEF-2 uses GTP to translocate peptidyl-tRNA and the ribosome along mRNA during elongation.

Eukaryotic elongation factor 2 (eEF-2) is required for the translocation of peptidyl-tRNA along the
mRNA during translation.
The elongation reaction requires GTP hydrolysis. The corresponding elongation factor in bacteria
is EF-G. Diphtheria toxin ADP-ribosylates eEF-2, leading to its inactivation.
Other options:
Option B: Initiation of eukaryotic protein synthesis requires several initiation factors, designated
elF-1, eIF-2, etc.
Option C: Chloramphenicol inhibits prokaryotic peptidyl transferase.
Option D: Peptidyl transferase is an rRNA (within the large ribosomal subunit) involved in
formation of the peptide bond between the amino acid groups within the A and P sites of the
ribosome.
emphasis: eEF-2 uses GTP to translocate peptidyl-tRNA and the ribosome along mRNA during elongation

rationales.b: Initiation uses eukaryotic initiation factors such as eIFs; eEF-2 functions later during elongation.
rationales.c: Chloramphenicol targets the bacterial ribosome, not eEF-2; diphtheria toxin inactivates eEF-2.
rationales.d: The ribosome's peptidyl-transferase center catalyzes peptide-bond formation; eEF-2 drives translocation.
